issues.legal_issue: An income-tax officer may record a partition when joint family property is divided in definite portions between groups of family members, even if the property allotted to one group has not been divided among that group’s members.
material_facts: A decree allocated separate properties to one family member and other properties collectively to his wife and three sons, who held those properties as tenants in common.
The member took possession of the properties allotted to him, separating them from the properties allotted to the other group.
The other group’s properties were not divided among its members, although the decree declared them divided inter se.
issues.conclusion: The conditions for recording a partition were satisfied because the property was divided in definite portions between the two groups; a complete partition among every family member was not required.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25A(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 authorizes an order recording partition if the family property is divided among members or groups of members in definite portions. A complete partition among all members is unnecessary. “Definite portions” generally requires physical division where the property admits of it, with division assessed in light of the nature of the property. The Court relied on Gordhandas T. Mangaldas v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay, 11 I.T.R. 183.

predicates.partition_recording_application: A family or one of its members applied to the tax officer to record a partition.
predicates.property_divided_into_definite_portions: The family property was separated into definite portions, with the form of division suited to the nature of the property.
predicates.division_between_member_groups: The property was allotted separately between groups of family members, even though members within a group did not divide their allotted property among themselves.

issues.definition: When an application concerns property divided into definite portions between member groups, the tax officer may record the partition.

issues.legal_issue: After a partition has been recorded, the original family cannot be assessed as an undivided family unless the order recording partition is set aside, though a group may be assessed separately if it independently constitutes an undivided family under personal law.
material_facts: An order recorded the partition between the original family member and the group consisting of his wife and sons.
The decree declared the wife and sons divided inter se and holding their allotted property as tenants in common.
The tax officer later assessed the group as though the original undivided family continued to exist; there was no evidence that the group independently formed an undivided family under personal law.
issues.conclusion: The original family could not be assessed as an undivided family after the partition order; the later assessments on that basis were incorrect.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 25A(3) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, an undivided family that has separated under personal law continues to be assessed as such only while no order under section 25A(1) has been recorded. Once an order is recorded, the original family ceases to exist for income-tax purposes and cannot be assessed in that status unless a competent authority sets the order aside. A group may be assessed as an undivided family if its members independently have that relationship under personal law.

predicates.recorded_partition_order: A tax officer recorded an order recognizing that family property had been partitioned.
predicates.later_assessment_as_original_undivided_f: A tax officer later assessed the family as though the original undivided family continued to exist.
predicates.order_set_aside: A competent authority set aside the order recording the partition.

issues.definition: If a partition order has been recorded and not set aside, a later assessment cannot treat the original family as an undivided family.

issues.legal_issue: A reassessment proceeding cannot be used to review or disregard an existing order recording partition.
material_facts: After a partition order had been recorded, a tax officer initiated reassessment proceedings on the ground that family income had escaped assessment.
The officer sought to assess the group as the original undivided family by disregarding the partition order.
The partition order had not been set aside by a competent authority.
issues.conclusion: The reassessment proceedings could not be used to ignore or review the partition order; the appropriate course was to seek action by the Commissioner to set it aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 confers no general power to review an order under section 25A(1), which operates for subsequent years. The Court agreed with Commissioner of Income-tax, Delhi and Rajasthan v. Ganeshi Lal Shyam Lal, 61 I.T.R. 408, that the proper course is to seek action by the Commissioner under section 33B to set aside the partition order. The ordinary rule that each assessment year is a self-contained period does not permit an officer to disregard such an order.

rule.if: reassessment_case and recorded_partition_order and reassessment_disregards_partition_order and not order_set_aside

predicates.reassessment_case: A tax officer initiated a proceeding to reassess income said to have escaped assessment.
predicates.recorded_partition_order: A tax officer had previously recorded an order recognizing that family property had been partitioned.
predicates.reassessment_disregards_partition_order: In reassessment, the tax officer treated the family as continuing undivided despite the recorded partition order.
predicates.order_set_aside: A competent authority set aside the order recording the partition.

issues.definition: In a reassessment proceeding, an order recording partition cannot be disregarded unless a competent authority has set it aside.
